chapter_theme: The invocation praises the omniscient one, free of birth and its three companions, whose word ends the suffering of souls, as the only god; the poet then makes his apology to the assembly (his work came in a dream and, like the moon, may carry a spot) and sums up the story to come: the demoness Neelakesi, unable to break a sage's penance, takes the great one's dharma, turns from violence and sets out to answer the schools, beginning with the view that accepts flesh.

cast.role: the demoness of the burning-ground temple who takes the Jain dharma and becomes its debater
the Jain sage whose penance Neelakesi cannot break
the lesser demons who seek out Neelakesi for help

1.reading: The poet praises as god the one whom the good worship, who has none of the four that begin with birth, whose word removes the suffering of souls and makes them rise to joy, the ancient lamp of dharma who knows all things.
1.nuance: The verse does not name the Jina; it defines god by marks (freedom from birth and the three that follow it, omniscience, a teaching that ends suffering) rather than by creation or grace. That this is the Jain omniscient teacher rests on those marks and on the later verses that name the Jina (சினவரன், 148); the claim is tagged Jain on that basis. The god acts through his word (சொல்), not by intervening.

claims.claim: only the omniscient one, free of birth and its companions, whose teaching ends the suffering of souls, is to be praised as god

2.reading: Those who have drunk the nectar of dharma he gave need not be named one by one; out of a devotion built by bowing over many days, the poet says, there is one thing he has to tell here.
2.nuance: Line 2 (இன்னார் இனையர் என வேண்டுவது இல்லை) can mean that the saints are too well known to need naming, or that no distinction of persons matters for those who drink the dharma; the reading is not fixed.

3.reading: The poet asks the learned not to throw his work aside in anger as speech not found in the old Agama: he bowed at the broad feet of the one who walked on cool lotuses, lay down, and saw it in a dream, and tells it as he saw it.
3.nuance: The apology anticipates the charge that a debate poem is a novelty outside scripture, and answers it by vision rather than by citing a text.
3.event: The poet bows at the lotus-walker's feet, lies down and sees the work in a dream.

4.reading: Neelakesi, a demoness in the form of a woman with dark kohl-lined eyes who did unrestrained harm, took the great one's dharma; her dark and evil heart turned, she rose into holiness, and she had the glory of turning the whole wide world from violence.
4.nuance: The verse plays on நீல (dark) three times: her name, the dark eyes, and the dark heart that turns. The conversion is the cause of her public work; the debates are framed as the reform of a world's violence (மறம்), not as a scholastic contest.
4.event: Neelakesi the demoness takes the great one's dharma, is transformed, and turns the world from violence.

claims.claim: taking the great one's dharma can turn even a demon's evil heart toward holiness

5.reading: The poet says he became clear as the god taught, took all he then understood as great, and, with his own ignorance as his only strength, set out to establish it in the assembly of eloquent poets, where none will now fault the verse.
5.nuance: The last line can be read as confidence (no one will now scorn the verse, since its matter is the god's) or as a hope; மாவென்று கொண்டேன் in line 2 is also open.
5.event: The poet, taught by the god, sets out to present his work before the assembly of poets.

6.reading: Even the white moon that the sea-girt world beholds and loves every day is not spotless; so the poet will not ask that all his words be taken as merit, and if there is a fault here, he will not refuse to own it.
6.nuance: A conventional apology to the assembly, but turned: the moon's spot is used to claim the right to a fault, not to be ashamed of it.

claims.claim: nothing, not even the moon, is free of flaw, so a work may be accepted with its faults acknowledged

7.reading: Since people take as meaningful even the cry of a bird, the poet argues, the world, if it wants dharma of excellent virtue, should not discard this work as speech fit for scorn but accept it.
7.nuance: Line 1 (தெள்ளி நரைத்துத் தெருளாது உறு தீமை செய்யும்) is obscure: it may describe the bird, or those who, though grey and learned, act without understanding. The argument is a fortiori: if a bird's call is heeded as an omen, a teaching of dharma deserves a hearing.

claims.claim: those who want dharma should judge a teaching by its worth, not scorn it for its humble source

8.reading: The lesser demons, who went searching through country, king, city and the forest around it because their god's refuge had been taken away, went and seized on the great demoness, and she, in enmity, tried many times to frighten the sage.
8.nuance: கடவுள் புகல் நீக்குதல் (the removing of refuge in the god) refers back, in the story told later (35 to 45), to the sage stopping the blood offering at the goddess's shrine; the verse compresses that, and the one she frightens is not named here.
8.event: The lesser demons, deprived of their offerings, seek out Neelakesi, who repeatedly tries to frighten the sage.

9.reading: Unable to disturb the penance of the one she had seen, she took the form of a woman with a doe's glance, and after she gave up violence, all that followed, beginning with the view that accepts flesh, the poet will tell to the assembly as he saw it.
9.nuance: ஊன் கொண்ட காட்சி (the view that has taken flesh) names the first debate by its issue, the eating of flesh, which the Kundalakesi debate charges against the Buddhist teaching (163); the poem's polemic is announced through an ethical charge before any metaphysics.
9.event: Failing to break the sage's penance, Neelakesi takes a woman's form and gives up violence; the poet announces the debates to follow.

links.note: Both invocations make knowledge the mark of the god: the Kural's வாலறிவன் (one of pure knowledge), the Neelakesi's எல்லாம் உணர்ந்தான் (one who knows all).
links.teaches: The Kural's unnamed pure knower is open enough that a Jain poet can fill the same slot with a god defined only by omniscience and freedom from birth, with no creating role.

gains.a: the Jain invocation is seen standing in a shared Tamil form of praising the god as knower
gains.b: the couplet's sectless epithet is shown being read in a sectarian sense by a debate poem

links.note: Both honour the feet of one who walked on the flower: மலர்மிசை ஏகினான் in the Kural, தண்டாமரைமேல் நடந்தான் in the Neelakesi.
links.teaches: An avowedly Jain poet uses the flower-walking epithet for his god, so the Kural's disputed epithet was current in Jain praise and not only open to other readings.

gains.a: the dream-apology is anchored in a known image of the god's feet
gains.b: the couplet's contested epithet gains a sectarian witness for one of its readings

links.note: Both use the moon's spot: the Naladiyar to say the noble cannot bear one stain as the moon does, the Neelakesi to say a work, like the moon, may carry a fault and still be loved.
links.teaches: The same image yields opposite counsel: for a person's character a single stain is unbearable, but for a poet before an assembly an acknowledged fault is excusable.

gains.a: the poet's apology is seen to lower the standard the ethics books set for the noble
gains.b: the quatrain's rule is shown to be about moral stain, not every imperfection

links.note: The Kural says a fault in the well-born shows like the moon's spot; the Neelakesi says the moon's spot does not stop the world loving it.
links.teaches: Read together, the moon's spot is both what makes a high fault visible and what proves the loved and high are never spotless, so visibility is not the same as rejection.

gains.a: the apology answers the worry the couplet raises, that a fault in a high place is seen by all
gains.b: the couplet's warning is softened by a case where the visible spot is forgiven

links.note: The invocation says she took the great one's dharma and her dark heart turned; at the end of the sermon she says she has taken the clear knowledge and asks for atonement for the wrong she did.
links.teaches: The prologue's single word of conversion becomes, in the story, a confession and a request for expiation, so the turn is shown as moral repair and not only a change of belief.

links.note: The invocation's demons who lost their god's refuge are, in the story, the demons who complain to Neelakesi that the sage stopped their offerings.
links.teaches: The phrase 'removing refuge in the god' turns out to mean ending blood offerings, so the demons' grievance is the loss of sacrifice, the poem's first act against killing.

links.note: The invocation's 'unable to disturb his penance' is told at length when her terrors fail and she gives up, fearing his penance will burn her.
links.teaches: The story makes the sage's penance an active power that the demoness fears, which the prologue's bare statement of her failure does not convey.

links.note: The invocation announces the debates 'beginning with the view that accepts flesh'; in the Kundalakesi debate Neelakesi charges the Buddha's path with not calling flesh-eating a fault.
links.teaches: The prologue names the Buddhist teaching by its tolerance of flesh, showing that the poem's first and framing charge against a rival school is ethical before it is metaphysical.

source_issues: Verse 7, line 3: 'திறத்த.: துரை' renders the aytham as '.:'; read திறத்தஃது உரை.
